items.title: Replay ordering depends on coordinates absent from the index row
items.statement: The event-record index says replay ordering uses segment generation and segment order, but neither coordinate is stored in the key or value schema. The excerpt also provides no append-to-index atomicity, projector checkpoint, duplicate resolution, or reconciliation rule, so crash recovery and concurrent projection can produce an index that cannot deterministically realize its stated ordering contract.

evidence.exact_quote: "replay_behavior": "Index row points back to authoritative seglog bytes and is rebuildable; replay ordering uses segment generation, segment order, offset, and sequence_id.",

items.impact: Replay and rebuild can diverge after crashes, duplicate projection, segment rollover, or concurrent writes.
items.builder_discretion: Implementation may choose transactional indexing or an idempotent reconciler, but the persisted ordering coordinates and externally testable recovery invariant are specification decisions.

items.title: Hash and segment-pointer fields accept structurally invalid values
items.statement: payload_sha256 is constrained only as a non-empty string, segment_ref is an arbitrary non-empty string, and byte_offset has no segment-bound or record-bound relationship. Corrupt or untrusted rows can therefore pass the value schema while pointing outside the segment or carrying a non-hash, with no specified quarantine or recovery response.
items.impact: Lookup, audit, and replay may consume malformed pointers or fail late and ambiguously.
items.builder_discretion: The validation mechanism is discretionary; the digest syntax, pointer bounds, and failure oracle are not.

items.title: Project-node replacement key has no monotonic race guard
items.statement: blocked_projection collapses all run-scoped states for a project/node into one canonical row, but the value contains no blocked sequence, source sequence, revision, generation, or compare-and-swap token. Delayed projectors and concurrent runs can overwrite a newer blocked or recovered state with an older one.

evidence.exact_quote: "migration": "Run-scoped blocked_projection.{run_id}.{node_id}.{blocked_sequence} keys are migration-read aliases only; canonical writes use v1 project/node key.",

items.impact: The UI and mutation gate can regress to stale truth or incorrectly re-enable/disable work.
items.builder_discretion: Revision representation is discretionary; the winner rule and stale-write rejection oracle must be canonical.

items.title: Blocked state has no explicit clear or supersession transition
items.statement: The family materializes blocked state and describes rebuild behavior, but defines no unblocked/tombstone state, deletion authority, superseding event, or atomic relationship between recovery completion and row removal. Consumers cannot distinguish currently blocked from orphaned historical state after recovery.

evidence.exact_quote: "replay_behavior": "Projection rebuilds from EventRecord/receipt sources; stale or degraded projections block mutation-capable actions.",

items.impact: Recovered nodes can remain indefinitely blocked, or a row may be deleted before recovery is durably certified.
items.builder_discretion: Tombstone versus deletion is discretionary; transition authority, ordering, and crash oracle are not.

items.title: Freshness and health combinations lack cross-field validity rules
items.statement: projection_freshness and projection_health are independently enumerated, allowing contradictory combinations such as current/unavailable or unavailable/healthy. No relation constrains last_projected_at_utc against blocked_at_utc or source events, so consumers have no deterministic precedence rule for misleading combinations.
items.impact: Different consumers can render or enforce different truths from the same row.
items.builder_discretion: The encoding can remain two fields, but allowed combinations and consumer precedence need specification.

items.title: Approval scope and allowed actions are not bound by an authority invariant
items.statement: approval_scope_key may be absent or null while allowed_action_ids is independently optional, and neither is bound to blocked_family, reason code, recovery target, actor, expiry, or authorizing receipt. A row can therefore appear to authorize actions without a verifiable scope or provenance.
items.impact: Mutation-capable consumers may over-authorize recovery or action paths from an unauthenticated projection field.
items.builder_discretion: The authorization engine is discretionary; required provenance and fail-closed validity are not.

items.title: Path privacy rule is prose-only and not representable by the schema
items.statement: The rule permits redacted or ref-only file paths under export policy, but dirty_file_paths and conflict_file_paths accept arbitrary strings and carry no per-value representation tag. redaction_profile cannot prove that stored strings are references rather than raw sensitive local paths.

evidence.exact_quote: "redaction_no_secret_rule": "File paths may be redacted or ref-only under export policy; raw secret content and credentials are invalid.",

items.impact: Sensitive filesystem topology, usernames, or secret-bearing names can be durably stored or exported while the row claims a safe profile.
items.builder_discretion: Tokenization mechanics are discretionary; the safe representation and validation oracle are not.

items.title: Source event evidence can be empty, duplicated, or malformed
items.statement: source_event_ids is required but allows an empty array, duplicate elements, and empty strings. This defeats the stated rebuild-from-source contract and leaves no falsifiable minimum evidence for a blocked projection.
items.impact: A projection may be accepted as rebuildable and auditable with no usable source evidence.
items.builder_discretion: Collection type is discretionary; non-empty, unique, valid identifiers and verification behavior are not.

items.title: Variable-length identifiers and arrays have no scale limits
items.statement: Core identifiers, action lists, source-event lists, and file-path lists have no maximum lengths or item counts. A corrupt or adversarial row can force unbounded decode, allocation, rendering, logging, and export work in tier-zero consumers.
items.impact: Storage, rebuild, UI, and support surfaces are vulnerable to memory, latency, or output amplification.
items.builder_discretion: Exact operational limits require specification-backed sizing; truncation and rejection behavior also need an oracle.

items.title: Projection health is not operationally diagnosable
items.statement: The row stores only a last-projected timestamp plus coarse freshness and health enums. It has no last applied source position, lag, rebuild generation/progress, error code, retry state, or diagnostic reference, so operators cannot determine whether a stale/degraded block is advancing, stuck, or safe to repair.
items.impact: Support cannot distinguish expected rebuild delay from corruption or stalled projection without unrelated state.
items.builder_discretion: Telemetry transport is discretionary; durable diagnostic identity and support oracles are not.

items.title: Opaque reason codes do not define accessible or localized disabled truth
items.statement: Planning Wizard disabled reason is a named consumer, yet blocked_reason_code is only a non-empty string and the row has no stable message key, parameter contract, severity, remediation label, or accessible announcement semantics. Unknown or malformed codes can yield blank, untranslated, or misleading UI while actions remain blocked.
items.impact: Users may not understand why an action is disabled or how to recover, and assistive technology may not announce a state change.
items.builder_discretion: Copy and presentation are discretionary; stable localization parameters, fallback behavior, and accessible state semantics are not.

items.title: Mutation blocking names no enforcement boundary or destructive-action matrix
items.statement: The replay prose says stale or degraded projections block mutation-capable actions, but the listed consumers do not identify the authoritative enforcement point, which actions are mutation-capable, whether unavailable also blocks, or how read-only/export/emergency recovery actions behave. UI disablement alone could be bypassed and different consumers can fail open differently.

evidence.exact_quote: "replay_behavior": "Projection rebuilds from EventRecord/receipt sources; stale or degraded projections block mutation-capable actions.",

items.impact: A stale or degraded projection can be bypassed or can over-block safe recovery, depending on caller interpretation.
items.builder_discretion: Enforcement architecture is discretionary; authoritative caller coverage and fail-closed behavior are not.

items.title: Legacy alias migration has no collision or retirement oracle
items.statement: Run-scoped rows become migration-read aliases while the canonical key drops run and blocked sequence. The excerpt does not define which legacy row wins, how multiple runs merge, whether canonical data supersedes aliases, how failed migration rolls back, or when aliases may be retired.

evidence.exact_quote: "migration": "Run-scoped blocked_projection.{run_id}.{node_id}.{blocked_sequence} keys are migration-read aliases only; canonical writes use v1 project/node key.",

items.impact: Migration can nondeterministically resurrect old blocks, lose concurrent-run evidence, or diverge across readers.
items.builder_discretion: Migration mechanism is discretionary; precedence, completeness, rollback, and retirement criteria are not.

items.title: Event payload authority and index retention boundary are explicit
items.statement: The excerpt explicitly makes seglog bytes authoritative, limits compaction by authoritative retention, and excludes payload bytes from the index. This closes the basic source-of-truth and payload-duplication ambiguity, although it does not close the ordering and atomicity gap recorded separately.

evidence.exact_quote: "retention_compaction": "Rebuildable index may compact only after authoritative seglog retention permits it.",
"redaction_no_secret_rule": "Index stores only ids, offsets, hashes, and refs; payload bytes stay in seglog under EventRecord redaction rules.",

items.title: Closed object schemas reject unknown properties
items.statement: Both value schemas set additionalProperties to false and enumerate required properties, providing a clear structural rejection baseline for unknown fields and missing required fields.

items.title: Fail-closed behavior for stale or degraded projection is explicit
items.statement: The excerpt explicitly requires stale or degraded projections to block mutation-capable actions. This is a useful fail-closed baseline, subject to the separate enforcement-boundary and invalid-combination gaps.

dimension_assessments.summary: Consumers are named, but the authoritative reconciliation and mutation-enforcement callers are not.
Contradictory freshness/health combinations and the absent unblocked transition leave invalid or ambiguous states.
The canonical project/node row has no revision or winner rule, and event indexing lacks an atomicity contract.
No crash boundary or reconciliation oracle binds seglog append to index projection or recovery to projection clearing.
Clear/supersession and migration rollback behavior are unspecified.
Allowed actions lack verifiable approval provenance and the enforcing authority is unnamed.
The event index establishes a useful no-payload boundary, but blocked-projection path redaction is not schema-verifiable.
Digest, segment-pointer, identifier, evidence-array, and path values accept malformed or resource-amplifying content.
Invalid projection-state combinations and opaque disabled reason codes can render misleading GUI truth.
The excerpt defines local redb/seglog persistence and no network operation; network-loss behavior cannot be required from this bounded storage window.
No bounds constrain variable-length strings or arrays consumed by tier-zero storage, UI, rebuild, or support paths.
The Wizard-facing disabled state lacks accessible announcement and fallback semantics.
Opaque reason strings have no stable localization key, parameter, or unknown-code fallback contract.
Legacy read aliases lack collision precedence, completeness, rollback, and retirement criteria.
Coarse state and one timestamp cannot diagnose projection lag, rebuild progress, or errors.
A fail-closed baseline exists, but the destructive-action matrix and authoritative enforcement point are absent.
Owner and schema references exist, but replay coordinates, authorization provenance, GUI reason semantics, and enforcement ownership are not closed in this authoritative core.
There are no oracles for stale-write rejection, index reconciliation, valid pointer bounds, source evidence minimums, state clearing, or migration completion.

The bounded excerpt cannot establish runtime validator format enforcement, transaction semantics, or out-of-window consumer behavior; the identified seams remain unresolved within the authorized evidence.
